explanation: das Land kan betyde et land eller landdistriktet uden for byen.
Ved et territorium med grænser betyder det „land“.
I modsætning til byen betyder auf dem Land „på landet“.
Konteksten afgør betydningen.

examples.de: Ich komme aus einem kleinen Land.
examples.lv: Jeg kommer fra et lille land.

examples.de: Auf dem Land ist es ruhig.

comparison.example: Deutschland ist ein Land. – Tyskland er et land.
Ich wohne in der Stadt. – Jeg bor i byen.
Er wohnt in einem Dorf. – Han bor i en landsby.
Die Erde ist rund. – Jorden er rund.

tip.text: Land som stat → das Land; området uden for byen → auf dem Land.

important: aufs Land betyder „ud på landet“, ikke „til et land“.
das Land er ikke det samme som die Stadt.

study.explanation: ab marks the starting point of a period, route or applicability and often means “from” or “starting at”.

comparison.meaning: from a starting point in time or place
comparison.example: ab Montag – from Monday

comparison.meaning: from a person, source or point
comparison.example: von mir – from me
aus dem Haus – out of the house

tip.text: A starting point in time or place → ab.

important: ab marks when or where something starts.
For origin or movement out of something, von or aus is usually used.

study.explanation: aber introduces a contrast or objection and usually means “but” or “however”.

examples.de: Ich möchte mitkommen, aber ich habe keine Zeit.
examples.lv: I would like to come along, but I do not have time.

examples.de: Das Essen war lecker, aber zu teuer.
examples.lv: The food was delicious, but too expensive.

examples.de: Er hat recht, aber ich sehe das anders.
examples.lv: He is right, but I see it differently.

comparison.example: Ich komme, aber später. – I am coming, but later.
Ich wollte keinen Tee, sondern Kaffee. – I did not want tea, but coffee.
Es ist kalt, jedoch sonnig. – It is cold, but sunny.

tip.text: A general contrast → aber; a correction after nicht/kein → sondern.

important: aber expresses a contrast or objection.
For “not … but rather …”, German normally uses sondern.

study.explanation: an is used for contact with or proximity to a vertical surface, edge, boundary or body of water.

comparison.example: an der Wand – on the wall
auf dem Tisch – on the table

comparison.meaning: at someone’s place or near a place
comparison.example: beim Arzt – at the doctor’s

tip.text: At a wall, window, edge or body of water → an.

important: an is not a general translation of every English “at”.
For a horizontal surface, German usually uses auf.

explanation: ein is the indefinite article for masculine and neuter nouns in the nominative.
Masculine: ein Mann; neuter: ein Buch.
The feminine form is eine.
The masculine accusative form is einen.

examples.lv: He is looking for a pen.

comparison.example: Ein Mann wartet. – A man is waiting.
Eine Frau wartet. – A woman is waiting.
Ich habe ein Buch. – I have a book.
Ich sehe einen Mann. – I see a man.

tip.text: An unspecified person or thing → ein/eine; masculine accusative → einen.

important: ein is an indefinite article, not a definite article.
For something already identified, der, die or das is often required.
Feminine: eine; masculine accusative: einen.

explanation: das Eis can mean both frozen water and ice cream.
For frozen water, English says “ice”.
For the dessert, English says “ice cream”.
The context shows which meaning is intended.

examples.lv: I am eating an ice cream.
Would you like an ice cream?

examples.de: Im Winter liegt Eis auf dem See.
examples.lv: In winter, there is ice on the lake.

examples.de: Ich nehme ein Eis mit Schokolade.
examples.lv: I’ll have a chocolate ice cream.

comparison.example: Ich esse ein Eis. – I am eating an ice cream.
Der Schnee ist weiß. – The snow is white.
Das Wasser ist kalt. – The water is cold.
Eis ist ein Dessert. – Ice cream is a dessert.

tip.text: Food or dessert → ice cream; frozen water → ice.

important: English uses two words, “ice” and “ice cream”, while German often uses das Eis for both.
The context distinguishes the meanings.

explanation: erst often means “only” or “not until” when a time, age or stage is later or lower than expected.
In a sequence, erst can mean “first”.
Ich bin erst 18. = I am only 18.
Erst lernen, dann spielen. = Study first, then play.

examples.lv: I am not coming until tomorrow.

examples.de: Wir essen erst um acht Uhr.
examples.lv: We are not eating until eight o’clock.

comparison.example: Erst lernen, dann spielen. – Study first, then play.
Zuerst frühstücken wir. – First, we have breakfast.

comparison.meaning: only, limiting an amount or choice
comparison.example: Ich habe nur 5 Euro. – I only have 5 euros.
Dann gehen wir nach Hause. – Then we go home.

tip.text: A time, age or stage → erst; a limited amount or choice → nur.

important: erst and nur can both translate as “only”, but they are not interchangeable.
erst commonly concerns time, sequence, age or a stage not yet reached.
zuerst normally means “first” in a neutral sequence.

explanation: es is the German neuter pronoun “it”.
It is also used as an impersonal subject in expressions about weather or general conditions.
With a neuter noun, es can refer back to that noun.
info: German es usually corresponds to English “it”.
In weather expressions, English and German both use an impersonal subject.

comparison.example: Es regnet. – It is raining.
Ich lerne Deutsch. – I am learning German.

tip.text: German es = English it; German ich = English I.

important: Do not confuse German es with the Latvian pronoun es.
German es often means “it” or serves as an impersonal subject.

explanation: essen is a verb meaning “to eat”.
It describes the action of consuming food.
The capitalised noun das Essen means “food” or “meal”.
Verb and noun are distinguished by capitalisation and context.

examples.lv: What do you want to eat?

important: essen is a verb and is written with a lower-case e.
das Essen is a noun and is written with a capital E.

explanation: etwas means “something” when it replaces an unspecified thing.
Before an adjective or an uncountable amount, it can mean “a little” or “somewhat”.
The context determines the meaning.

examples.lv: I would like something to drink.

comparison.example: Ich brauche etwas. – I need something.
Willst du was trinken? – Would you like something to drink?
Ich bin ein bisschen müde. – I am a little tired.
Ich brauche nichts. – I need nothing.

tip.text: An unspecified thing → something; a degree → a little / somewhat.

important: etwas means “something”; nichts means “nothing”.
etwas trinken = to drink something.

explanation: With a noun, ganz means “whole” or “entire”.
Before an adjective or adverb, it can mean “completely” or “quite”.
ganz is not the pronoun alles (“everything”).

comparison.example: der ganze Tag – the whole day
Alles ist gut. – Everything is fine.

tip: Before a noun, ganz often means “whole” or “entire”.
Before an adjective, it often means “completely” or “quite”.
important: der ganze Tag = the whole day.
alles is the pronoun “everything”.

explanation: klein means “small” or “little” in size, extent or age.
It can describe a room, object, child or other person.
The inflected form changes with the noun: eine kleine Tasche.
tip: Pay attention to adjective endings: klein, kleine, kleinen.
important: klein describes small size, extent or young age.
It does not mean “a small amount”; dafür German often uses wenig.

explanation: nach means “to” with cities and most countries without an article.
With time or sequence, it means “after” or “past”.
In nach Hause, it means “home”.
The preposition takes the dative case.

examples.de: Nach dem Essen gehen wir spazieren.
examples.lv: After the meal, we go for a walk.

comparison.example: Ich fahre nach Berlin. – I am travelling to Berlin.

comparison.meaning: to a person or specific destination
comparison.example: Ich gehe zum Arzt. – I am going to the doctor.

comparison.meaning: into/to a place used with an article
comparison.example: Ich gehe in die Schule. – I am going to school.
Vor dem Essen wasche ich mir die Hände. – Before the meal, I wash my hands.

tip.text: nach Hause; nach Berlin; nach dem Essen; zehn nach acht.

important: nach is not used with every destination.
“To school” is normally in die Schule, not nach Schule.

explanation: nehmen means “to take” or “to choose”.
It is used when someone takes, selects or uses something.
bringen means “to bring” something to a person or place.
holen means “to fetch” by going somewhere and bringing something back.

examples.lv: I am bringing you the book.

comparison.example: Nimm das Buch! – Take the book!
Ich bringe dir das Buch. – I am bringing you the book.
Ich hole Wasser. – I am fetching water.
Ich nehme dich mit. – I am taking you with me.

tip.text: Take or choose something → nehmen; bring it somewhere → bringen; fetch it → holen.

important: Ich nehme den Bus means “I take the bus”.
nehmen is not the same as bringen or holen.

explanation: ob introduces an indirect yes/no question and usually means “whether” or “if”.
It is used after verbs such as fragen, wissen or sehen.
For a direct choice between alternatives, German uses oder.
In an ob-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end.

examples.de: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt.
examples.lv: I do not know whether he is coming.

examples.de: Sie fragt, ob du Zeit hast.
examples.lv: She asks whether you have time.
Tell me whether that is true.
Are you coming today or tomorrow?

comparison.meaning: whether / if in an indirect question
comparison.example: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. – I do not know whether he is coming.
Kaffee oder Tee? – Coffee or tea?

comparison.meaning: if / when, expressing a condition or repeated time
comparison.example: Wenn du Zeit hast ... – If you have time ...
Ich weiß, dass er kommt. – I know that he is coming.

tip.text: I do not know whether... → ob; coffee or tea → oder.

important: ob does not express a direct “or” choice.
For alternatives, use oder, not ob.

explanation: sprechen means to speak, talk or use a language.
It can describe a language ability or a conversation.
The subject determines the form: ich spreche, sie spricht.

examples.lv: She is speaking with her teacher.

comparison.example: Wir sprechen über die Arbeit. – We are talking about work.

comparison.meaning: to say / tell a specific message
comparison.example: Sag mir die Wahrheit. – Tell me the truth.

tip: A specific statement or message → sagen.
important: sprechen describes speaking or a conversation.
It is not interchangeable with sagen in every context.

explanation: stehen means “to stand” or “to be upright”.
For a person, it describes a standing position.
For an object, it describes an upright position or location.
Contrast: stehen = stand, sitzen = sit, liegen = lie.

examples.lv: I am standing at the door.

examples.de: Der Stuhl steht in der Küche.
examples.lv: The chair is standing in the kitchen.
He is sitting at the table.

examples.de: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.lv: The book is lying on the table.

comparison.example: Ich stehe hier. – I am standing here.
Er sitzt am Tisch. – He is sitting at the table.
Das Buch liegt dort. – The book is lying there.
Ich stelle die Flasche hin. – I put the bottle down upright.

tip.text: Upright state → stehen; seated → sitzen; horizontal → liegen; placing upright → stellen.

important: stehen describes a state, not the action of placing something.
To put an object upright, use stellen.

explanation: zum is the contraction of zu and dem.
It is used with masculine and neuter nouns in the dative.
It usually indicates direction, destination or purpose.
In everyday German, zum normally replaces the full form zu dem.

examples.lv: I am going to the doctor.
We are going to the station.
She is going to the supermarket.
He is going to the airport.
We are going to the concert.
The present is for the birthday.
I am going to the hairdresser.

comparison.meaning: to the / for the (masculine or neuter)
comparison.example: zum Arzt – to the doctor
zur Schule – to school
zu Hause – at home

comparison.meaning: to cities and countries without an article
comparison.example: nach Berlin – to Berlin
beim Arzt – at the doctor’s

tip: For feminine nouns: zu + der → zur.
important: zum = zu dem with masculine or neuter nouns in the dative.
It normally marks a destination or purpose.
For feminine nouns, use zur: zur Bank, zur Post.
beim Arzt = at the doctor’s; zum Arzt = to the doctor.

study.translation: al • a la • sobre (contracción de auf das)
explanation: aufs es la contracción de la preposición auf y el artículo das.
La forma completa es auf das.
Se usa con sustantivos neutros para indicar movimiento hacia una superficie, un lugar o un acontecimiento.
Responde a wohin? (¿adónde?), no a wo? (¿dónde?).
En el uso corriente se prefiere aufs a la forma completa auf das.

examples.lv: Ella se sienta en el sofá.
Pon el bolso sobre la cama.
Pon el libro en la estantería.

comparison.meaning: al / a la / sobre, hacia una superficie o lugar neutro
comparison.example: aufs Dach – al tejado
auf den Tisch – sobre la mesa
an die Wand – a la pared
ins Zimmer – a la habitación
zum Arzt – al médico

tip: auf + das → aufs; expresa destino o dirección.
Para una ubicación sin movimiento se usa auf + dativo.
important: aufs solo contrae auf + das y se usa con sustantivos neutros.
No lo confundas con an para una superficie vertical ni con ins para entrar en un espacio.

explanation: dass introduce una oración subordinada que expresa un hecho, un pensamiento o algo dicho.
En español suele corresponder a la conjunción «que».
En la subordinada alemana introducida por dass, el verbo conjugado va al final.

examples.de: Ich weiß, dass du müde bist.

comparison.example: Ich weiß, dass er kommt. – Sé que viene.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet. – Me quedo en casa porque llueve.
Ich lerne Deutsch, damit ich in Deutschland arbeiten kann. – Estudio alemán para poder trabajar en Alemania.
Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt. – No sé si viene.

tip.text: La conjunción «que» → dass; el verbo alemán va al final de la subordinada.

important: dass significa «que» e introduce una subordinada.
No lo confundas con das, que puede ser artículo o pronombre.
